question_html:
Insert 6 into the following AVL tree and show the rebalancing procedure step by step.

The initial AVL tree has root 3, with left child 2 and right child 8. Node 2 has left child 1. Node 8 has left child 5 and right child 9. Node 5 has left child 4 and right child 7.
solution_html:
We insert 6 using the ordinary BST insertion procedure and we obtain the following tree:

Root 3, left child 2 (with left child 1), right child 8 (with left child 5, right child 9). Node 5 has left child 4 and right child 7. Node 7 has left child 6.

This tree is imbalanced at node 8 since it has a left subtree of height 3 and a right subtree of height 1, leading to a balance factor of 2. Note that the root node 3 is also imbalanced, but we always perform rotations on the lower levels first since this may fix the imbalances at higher levels.

Since node 8 has a taller left subtree and node 5 has a taller right subtree, this is a left-right imbalance so we must perform a double rotation on node 7 to correct it. We perform the first rotation (right rotation at node 5) to obtain:

Root 3, left child 2 (with left child 1), right child 8 (with left child 7, right child 9). Node 7 has left child 5. Node 5 has left child 4 and right child 6.

We then perform the second rotation (left rotation at node 8) and are left with:

Root 3, left child 2 (with left child 1), right child 7. Node 7 has left child 5 and right child 8. Node 5 has left child 4 and right child 6. Node 8 has right child 9.

This is a balanced tree, so we are done.

question_html:
Recall the algorithm for deleting an element from a binary search tree. If that element has no children, we do nothing. If it has one child, we can simply remove it and move its child upwards. Otherwise, if the node has two children, we replace the node we are deleting with its successor (and if the successor has one child, move the successor child upwards to be a child of the previous parent of the successor). This algorithm works because of the following fact: the successor of a node with two children has no left child. Prove this fact.

  • (a) First prove that the successor of a node \(x\) with two children must be contained in the right subtree of \(x\).
  • (b) Use this fact to prove that the successor of \(x\) cannot have a left child.
solution_html:
This problem is related to the correctness of the deletion operation in binary search trees.

(a) Let \(s\) denote the successor of \(x\). Recall that the successor of a node is the minimum value node that is greater than \(x\). Suppose for contradiction purposes that \(x\) and \(s\) have a common ancestor \(a \neq x, s\) such that \(x\) and \(s\) are in different subtrees of \(a\). Then as \(x < s\), it must be the case that \(x\) is in the left subtree of \(a\) and \(s\) is in the right subtree of \(a\). But this would imply that \(x < a < s\) which contradicts the fact that \(s\) is the successor of \(x\). Therefore it must be the case that either \(x\) is an ancestor of \(s\), or \(s\) is an ancestor of \(x\).

Suppose for contradiction purposes that \(s\) is an ancestor of \(x\). Then \(x\) must be in the left subtree of \(s\) as \(x < s\). Now let \(r\) denote the right child of \(x\). We have that \(x < r\). As \(r\) is in the left subtree of \(s\), we have that \(r < s\). Combining these two facts we get that \(x < r < s\), which contradicts the fact that \(s\) is the successor of \(x\). Therefore it must be the case that \(x\) is an ancestor of \(s\). And, as \(x < s\), \(s\) needs to be in the right subtree of \(x\).

(b) Suppose for contradiction purposes that \(s\) had a left child \(t\). By the BST property we have \(t < s\). But as \(t\) is contained in the right subtree of \(x\) by item (a), we also have that \(x < t\). Combining these two facts we get \(x < t < s\), which contradicts the fact that \(s\) is the successor of \(x\). Therefore the successor \(s\) of \(x\) cannot have a left child.

Putting the facts together: whenever we are deleting a BST node \(x\) that has two children and replacing it with its successor \(s\), \(s\) will either have no subtrees or only a right subtree (which can then be moved upwards to be a child of the previous parent of node \(s\)).

question_html:
We know that when inserting an element into a binary search tree, there is only one valid place to put that item in the tree (and that is an important property for the correctness of binary search trees). Let's prove this fact rigorously. Let \(T\) be a binary search tree and let \(x\) be an integer not contained in \(T\). Prove that exactly one of the following statements is true:

  • Statement 1: The successor of \(x\) has no left child.
  • Statement 2: The predecessor of \(x\) has no right child.

That is, prove that it cannot be the case that both of these statements are true simultaneously, nor that both of these statements are false simultaneously. This implies that there is a unique insertion point for \(x\) since upon insertion \(x\) must either become the left child of its successor or the right child of its predecessor.

Note: the fact that we are proving (that every element has a unique insertion point) is still true when the element we are inserting would be the minimum or maximum value in the tree, but the two statements we have given do not make sense in this case. Think about why this is true!
solution_html:
Let the predecessor of \(x\) be \(p\), and the successor be \(s\). We know that \(p < x < s\), and that there is no key \(k\) in the tree such that \(p < k < x\) or \(x < k < s\).

We claim that either \(s\) is an ancestor of \(p\), or \(p\) is an ancestor of \(s\). Suppose for contradiction that neither is an ancestor of the other, and therefore \(p\) and \(s\) have a common ancestor \(a\) such that \(p\) and \(s\) are in different subtrees of \(a\). Notice that in this case, as \(p < s\), \(p\) would need to be in the left subtree of \(a\) and \(s\) in the right subtree. Then we know that \(p < a < s\). As \(x\) is not in the tree and therefore \(x eq a\), that means that either \(p < a < x\) or \(x < a < s\). But by the definitions of successor and predecessor both of those cases are impossible. So we have a contradiction, meaning that either \(s\) is an ancestor of \(p\), or \(p\) is an ancestor of \(s\).

Case 1: \(s\) is an ancestor of \(p\). In this case, \(s\) has a left child as \(p\) needs to be in the left subtree of \(s\) by the properties of a BST, and thus Statement 1 is false. Assume for contradiction purposes that \(p\) has a right child denoted by \(r\). Since \(r\) is a right child of \(p\), it holds that \(p < r\). Since \(r\) is in the left subtree of \(s\), it holds that \(r < s\). Therefore \(p < r < s\). As \(x\) is not in the tree and therefore \(x eq r\), that means that either \(p < r < x\) or \(x < r < s\). But by the definitions of successor and predecessor both of those cases are impossible. So we have a contradiction and therefore \(p\) cannot have a right child, which implies that Statement 2 is true. Therefore, in the case in which \(s\) is an ancestor of \(p\), Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.

Case 2: \(p\) is an ancestor of \(s\). In this case, \(p\) has a right child as \(s\) needs to be in the right subtree of \(p\) by the properties of a BST, and thus Statement 2 is false. Assume for contradiction purposes that \(s\) has a left child denoted by \(\ell\). Since \(\ell\) is a left child of \(s\), it holds that \(\ell < s\). Since \(\ell\) is in the right subtree of \(p\), it holds that \(p < \ell\). Therefore \(p < \ell < s\). As \(x\) is not in the tree and therefore \(x eq \ell\), that means that either \(p < \ell < x\) or \(x < \ell < s\). But by the definitions of successor and predecessor both of those cases are impossible. So we have a contradiction and therefore \(s\) cannot have a left child, which implies that Statement 1 is true. Therefore, in the case in which \(p\) is an ancestor of \(s\), Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.

Notice that by following the insertion procedures of a BST, \(x\) will be inserted as a right child of \(p\) in the case in which \(s\) is an ancestor of \(p\), otherwise it will be inserted as a left child of \(s\).

question_html:
Consider the binary search tree shown below, with balance factors as indicated. Assume that the subtrees ST1, ST2, ST3 and ST4 are AVL trees. Show that performing the rotation algorithm for the right-left case results in an AVL tree.

The tree has root \(x\) with balance factor \(-2\). Node \(x\) has left subtree ST1 and right child \(z\) with balance factor \(1\). Node \(z\) has left child \(y\) with balance factor \(0\) and right subtree ST4. Node \(y\) has left subtree ST2 and right subtree ST3.
solution_html:
Let height(ST2) be \(h\). We can deduce that height(ST3), height(ST4) and height(ST1) are also \(h\) (based on the balance factors).

After applying the two phases of the right-left case rotations, we obtain the following tree:

Root \(y\) with balance factor \(0\). Node \(y\) has left child \(x\) with balance factor \(0\) and right child \(z\) with balance factor \(0\). Node \(x\) has left subtree ST1 and right subtree ST2. Node \(z\) has left subtree ST3 and right subtree ST4.

Based on the heights of ST1, ST2, ST3 and ST4 we can deduce the balance factors of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) as all being 0. Since ST1, ST2, ST3 and ST4 are AVL trees, the balance factors of all nodes in the tree are in \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\). So the tree is now an AVL tree.

question_html:
Consider the following 2-3 Search Tree:

The root is a 3-Node containing keys 15 and 51. The root has three children: a 3-Node containing 3 and 6 (with children: 2-Node 0, 3-Node 4 and 8 and 12, and 2-Node containing nothing shown for leaf level — actually leaf 2-Nodes 0, 4, 8 12), a 3-Node containing 19 and 28 (with leaf children 16 18, 23 25, 40), and a 2-Node containing 60 (with leaf children 59, and 3-Node 65 70).

More precisely: root [15, 51] with children [3,6], [19,28], [60]. Under [3,6]: leaves [0], [4], [8,12]. Under [19,28]: leaves [16,18], [23,25], [40]. Under [60]: leaves [59], [65,70].

  • (a) Visualise the state of the tree after sequentially performing each of the following actions:
    1. Insert key 5
    2. Insert key 62
    3. Delete key 59
    4. Insert key 10
    5. Delete key 40

    Note: We are only covering deletion if the key is a leaf node.

  • (b) Convert the resulting 2-3 Search Tree from part (a) into the equivalent Left-Leaning Red-Black Tree.
solution_html:
(a)

i. Insert key 5: We first traverse the tree to find where key 5 can be placed. The 2-Node leaf containing 4 is where key 5 can be inserted. Since it is a 2-Node, we simply add the new key by converting the leaf into a 3-Node. Result: leaf [4,5] replaces [4].

ii. Insert key 62: We traverse down the tree to find the position for 62. The path goes through root [15,51], then [60], then leaf [65,70]. We insert 62 into the 3-Node leaf [65,70], creating a 4-Node [62,65,70]. A 4-Node is not allowed — we promote the middle element (65) into the parent [60], making it [60,65], and leave 62 and 70 as individual 2-Node leaves. Result: internal node [60,65] with leaves [59], [62], [70].

iii. Delete key 59: To delete key 59 (a leaf), we must maintain the invariant that the node we are processing is larger than a 2-Node. We start at the root [15,51] which satisfies the invariant. We reach the 3-Node [60,65]. Our next target is the 2-Node leaf [59]. The immediate sibling of [59] is not a 2-Node (it is a 3-Node [60,65] from the parent perspective). We combine the two 2-Nodes and demote the current key 60 into a 4-Node [59,60,62]. Since we are at a leaf and it is larger than a 2-Node, we delete key 59. Result: internal node [65] with leaves [60,62] and [70].

iv. Insert key 10: A simple traversal finds key 10 belongs in the leaf [8,12] (a 3-Node). Inserting creates 4-Node [8,10,12]. We promote the middle element (10) into parent [3,6], making it [3,6,10] — another 4-Node. We promote middle element (6) into root [15,51], making it [6,15,51] — another 4-Node. Since the root becomes a 4-Node, we promote the middle element (15) as the new root. New root: [15], with children [6] and [51]. Under [6]: [3] and [10], with leaves [0], [4,5], [8], [12]. Under [51]: [19,28] and [65], with leaves [16,18], [23,25], [40], [60,62], [70].

v. Delete key 40: We process nodes top-down ensuring each is larger than a 2-Node. The root [15] is a 2-Node so we first process it: combine with children to form root as a 4-Node [6,15,51] temporarily. Then recurse to [19,28] (a 3-Node, satisfies invariant). Key 40 is in a 2-Node leaf. Its immediate sibling is 3-Node [23,25]. We rotate: move largest key of sibling (25) into parent, move relevant parent key (28) into the target node. Parent becomes [19,25], target becomes [28,40]. We delete 40. Result: leaf [28]. Finally, fix any remaining 4-Nodes on exit: root [6,15,51] promotes 15 as new root. Final tree: root [15], children [6] and [51]. Under [6]: [3] with leaves [0],[4,5] and [10] with leaves [8],[12]. Under [51]: [19,25] with leaves [16,18],[23],[28] and [65] with leaves [60,62],[70].

(b) The 2-3 Search Tree can be converted to the Left-Leaning Red-Black Tree as follows: 2-Nodes become black nodes; 3-Nodes are represented as a black node with a red left child. The equivalent LLRBT has root 15 (black). Left subtree: black 6, with red left child 3 (black children 0, 5 — where 5 is red left child of black 5... following the structural conversion). Right subtree rooted at black 51, with black 25 (red left child 19, which has red children 18 and 23), and black 65 (red left child 60, with children 62 and 70).

The full converted LLRBT (from the final 2-3 tree after all operations): root is black 15. Left child is black 6 (red left child 3, with black 0 and red-left-child structure for 4,5). Right child structure follows the 3-Node to black+red-left-child conversion rule throughout.

question_html:
Sequentially perform the following operations on an empty Left-Leaning Red-Black-Tree. For each operation: (1) draw the resulting Red-Black-Tree, (2) draw the equivalent 2-3 Search Tree, and (3) state the black height of the Red-Black-Tree.

  • (a) Insert key 40
  • (b) Insert key 20
  • (c) Insert key 5
  • (d) Insert key 1
  • (e) Insert key 32
  • (f) Insert key 64
  • (g) Insert key 13
  • (h) Insert key 5
  • (i) Insert key 38
  • (j) Insert key 36
solution_html:
When performing insertions into an LLRBT all nodes are inserted as red nodes. We then might need a sequence of left rotations, right rotations, or colour flips to maintain the properties of the tree. We keep recursively performing these back up to the root until all issues are fixed.

(a) Insert 40: Single red node 40. Since the root turns red we always turn it back to black. Result: black node 40. Black height = 0. Equivalent 2-3 tree: 2-Node [40].

(b) Insert 20: 20 becomes the red left child of 40. No other action needed. Black node 40 with red left child 20. Black height = 0. Equivalent 2-3 tree: 3-Node [20, 40].

(c) Insert 5: 5 becomes the red left child of 20. Node 40 has a red left child 20, and 20's left child is also red — perform a right rotation. After rotation: black 20 with red left child 5 and red right child 40. Since 20 has two red children, perform a colour flip: 20 stays black (as root), 5 and 40 become black. Black height = 1. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [5] and [40] (all 2-Nodes).

(d) Insert 1: 1 becomes the red left child of 5. No other action needed. Tree: black 20, left child black 5 (red left child 1), right child black 40. Black height = 1. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [1,5] and [40].

(e) Insert 32: 32 becomes the red left child of 40. No other action needed. Tree: black 20, left child black 5 (red left child 1), right child black 40 (red left child 32). Black height = 1. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [1,5] and [32,40].

(f) Insert 64: 64 becomes the red right child of 40. Now 40 has two red children (32 and 64) — colour flip: 40 becomes red, 32 and 64 become black. Now 20 has a red right child 40 — perform a left rotation. After rotation: root is black 40, left child red 20 (with left black 5 having red child 1, and right black 32), right child black 64. Black height = 1. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20,40] with children [1,5], [32], [64].

(g) Insert 13: 13 becomes the red right child of 5. Now 5 has two red children (1 and 13) — colour flip: 5 becomes red, 1 and 13 become black. Recursing up to 40: 40 has a red left child 20, and 20's left child 5 is also red — perform a right rotation at 40. After right rotation: root 20 (red), with left child red 5 and right child 40. Since 20 has two red children, flip colours: 20 red becomes root (turned black), 5 and 40 become black. Root black 20, left black 5 (black 1 and black 13), right black 40 (black 32 and black 64). Black height = 2. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [5] (leaves [1],[13]) and [40] (leaves [32],[64]).

(h) Insert 5 (duplicate): Following the insertion path, the key 5 already exists. The tree is unaltered. Black height = 2. Equivalent 2-3 tree unchanged.

(i) Insert 38: 38 becomes the red right child of 32. Since 32's only red child is a right child, perform a left rotation at 32. After rotation: 38 is black with red left child 32. Black height = 2. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [5] (leaves [1],[13]) and [40] (leaves [32,38],[64]).

(j) Insert 36: 36 becomes the red right child of 32 (which is now a red left child of 38). Since 32's only red child is a right child, perform a left rotation at 32. Then 38 has a red left child 36, and 36's left child 32 is also red — perform a right rotation at 38. Now 36 has two red children 32 and 38 — colour flip: 36 becomes red, 32 and 38 become black. Black height = 2. Equivalent 2-3 tree: root [20] with children [5] (leaves [1],[13]) and [40] (leaves [36,38] with children [32],[38], and [64]) — specifically under [40]: [36,40] node with leaves [32,38] and [64] restructured as the 2-3 equivalent.

The overall black height of the tree increases only when a red node is propagated up to the root, temporarily making the root red. Since we immediately change the root back to black, the black height increases by 1. This mirrors the process of passing up nodes in a 2-3 Search Tree.

question_html:
In the lecture recordings we claimed that AVL trees are good because the balance property guarantees that the tree always has height \(O(\log(n))\). Let's prove this.

  • (a) Write a recurrence relation for \(n(h)\), the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height \(h\). [Hint: It should be related to the Fibonacci numbers]
  • (b) Find an exact solution to this recurrence relationship in terms of the Fibonacci numbers. [Hint: Compare the sequence with the Fibonacci sequence, find a pattern, and then prove that your pattern is right using induction]
  • (c) Prove using induction that the Fibonacci numbers satisfy \(F(h) \geq 1.5^{h-1}\) for all \(h \geq 0\)
  • (d) Using (a), (b), and (c), prove that a valid AVL tree with \(n\) elements has height at most \(O(\log(n))\)
solution_html:
Consider an AVL tree of height \(h\) whose root node has the two subtrees \(L\) and \(R\). Suppose that \(L\) and \(R\) have the same height. We could remove the nodes from the lowest level of one of the two subtrees, making them differ in height by one and it would still be a valid AVL tree with the same height. Therefore an AVL tree with the fewest possible nodes must have \(L\) and \(R\) differing in height by one, hence they must have heights \(h-1\) and \(h-2\). Lastly, note that \(L\) and \(R\) must also be AVL trees with the fewest possible nodes. Therefore the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree satisfies the following recurrence relationship:

\[n(h) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } h = 0, \\ 2 & \text{if } h = 1, \\ 1 + n(h-1) + n(h-2) & \text{if } h > 0. \end{cases}\]

(b) This looks suspiciously similar to the Fibonacci sequence. Comparing the sequences:

\(h\)012345678
\(F(h)\)112358132134
\(n(h)\)12471220335488

This table strongly suggests the pattern \(n(h) = F(h+2) - 1\).

Let's prove this by induction. We have \(n(0) = F(2) - 1 = 1\) and \(n(1) = F(3) - 1 = 2\) as required. Now suppose \(n(h) = F(h+2) - 1\) for all \(h \leq k\) for some value of \(k\). We need to show that \(n(k+1) = F(k+3) - 1\). From the recurrence, we have \(n(k+1) = 1 + n(k) + n(k-1)\). Invoking the inductive hypothesis, we can write:

\[n(k+1) = 1 + F(k+2) - 1 + F(k+1) - 1 = F(k+2) + F(k+1) - 1\]

By the definition of Fibonacci numbers, \(F(k+2) + F(k+1) = F(k+3)\), hence we have \(n(k+1) = F(k+3) - 1\), as required. Hence by strong induction on \(k\), we have \(n(h) = F(h+2) - 1\) for all \(h\).

(c) We prove \(F(h) \geq 1.5^{h-1}\) for all \(h \geq 0\) by induction. Base cases: \(F(0) = 1 \geq 1.5^{-1}\) and \(F(1) = 1 \geq 1.5^{0}\). Now suppose \(F(h-1) \geq 1.5^{h-2}\) and \(F(h) \geq 1.5^{h-1}\). We need to prove \(F(h+1) \geq 1.5^{h}\). From the definition of Fibonacci numbers, \(F(h+1) = F(h) + F(h-1)\). Using the inductive hypothesis:

\[F(h+1) \geq 1.5^{h-1} + 1.5^{h-2} = 1.5 \times 1.5^{h-2} + 1.5^{h-2} = (1.5 + 1) \times 1.5^{h-2} \geq 2.25 \times 1.5^{h-2} = (1.5)^2 \times 1.5^{h-2} = 1.5^h\]

Therefore by induction on \(h\), we have \(F(h) \geq 1.5^{h-1}\) for all \(h\).

(d) Combining the above, we have \(n(h) = F(h+2) - 1 \geq 1.5^{h+1} - 1\). Rearranging, we find \(1.5^{h+1} \leq n(h) + 1\), and hence:

\[h + 1 \leq \log_{1.5}(n(h) + 1) \implies h = O(\log(n))\]

as required.
